newsitem.title: USA: Voters want divided government, could get gridlock.
newsitem.headline: Voters want divided government, could get gridlock.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Americans voters voted for divided government but they could end up getting bitter, partisan gridlock.
By re-electing President Bill Clinton but apparently returning Republican majorities in both houses of Congress, voters appeared to be signalling approval of the status quo.

After a bitter battle in 1995 during which the federal government was twice closed down over a budget confrontation, Clinton and the Republicans worked together on a number of pieces of major legislation as the 1996 election drew closer.
If voters expect more of the same in the next two years, they may be disappointed.
"I foresee a lot of conflict. The Republicans will certainly try to spoil Clinton's second term," said American University political scientist Allan Lichtman.

Republicans will keep control of the congressional committees investigating a wide range of alleged Clinton administration wrongdoing, including the complex Whitewater affair, the mishandling of the FBI files of some prominent Republicans and the latest revelations on campaign fundraising from foreign interests.

In Clinton's home town of Little Rock, independent counsel Kenneth Starr, a Republican, has been working with a Grand Jury, patiently building a case against many of Clinton's friends and allies for alleged Whitewater misdeeds.
He stopped issuing indictments in the runup to the election but that was a temporary pause and many believe his ultimate targets are Clinton himself and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton.
Clinton, in his victory speech, indicated he was willing to reach out to Republicans.

"It is time to put country ahead of party ... They (the voters) are sending us a message -- work together, meet our challenges, put aside the politics of division and build America's community together," he declared.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry looked forward to moderates of both parties joining hands to work with Clinton.
But Lichtman said neither Republicans elected to the Senate for the first time nor those re-elected to the House of Representatives were particularly moderate.

Bearing out his view, Republican congressional leaders were notably ungenerous on election night, vowing to pursue a wide range of inquiries into the president's political, business and personal affairs.

Republicans know they can expect to make more gains in the next congressional elections in 1998 because the party holding the White House traditionally loses seats in mid-term elections, especially when a president is serving his second term.

Politicians usually try to be a little gracious to their opponents, at least for one night when the voters have spoken. This year, even that convention seemed to have gone by the board, swallowed in bitterness.

Oklahoma Republican Senator Don Nickles said Republican control of Congress was "good news for cleaning up government when when we find that people are making mistakes in the White House. We're going to start watching them a little bit closer now."
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said voters were sending a Republican Congress back to keep Clinton under political lock and key.

In North Carolina, hardline Republican Jesse Helms said in his victory speech: "I can guarantee you one thing: there's going to be six more years of torment for (Massachusetts Democratic Senator) Ted Kennedy and all the rest of those other liberal Democrats."
Arizona Senator John McCain also trained his scorn on Vice President Al Gore, Clinton's heir apparent.

"Perhaps, tonight, after this campaign is over, the vice president of the United States, Captain Ozone, will tell the American people what he was doing in that Buddhist temple," he said, referring to Gore's attendance at a fundraising function for the Democratic Party in a Buddhist temple in California.
It was a sour evening for U.S. politics, promising a sour and harsh period to come.
